strengths: The central idea is novel and practically meaningful: partition-wise attention and the encoder/GroupSwap/decoder design avoid processing MASK tokens while retaining arbitrary-order parallel generation.

The efficiency evidence is strong within the evaluated setting. On 1024-token OpenWebText generation, PGM provides roughly 5–5.5× lower latency and higher throughput than MDLM at matched sampling-step counts, with comparable or better generative perplexity.

The evaluation covers two text datasets, downstream tasks, distillation, and a preliminary image experiment. It includes useful architecture, sampling, complementary-masking, precision, and training-cost analyses.
The paper identifies numerical-precision artifacts in masked-model sampling and evaluates all models using FP64 logits, strengthening the credibility of the comparisons.
The method and experimental setup are generally explained clearly, with sampling pseudocode, optimization details, computational costs, and a stated plan to release code and checkpoints.
weaknesses: The principal quality comparisons are not capacity- or compute-matched. On OpenWebText, the comparable 12-layer PGM underperforms MDLM, while improvements require more layers or a wider hidden dimension; exact parameter counts, FLOPs, and parameter-matched baselines are absent.

The empirical scope is limited to relatively small models and dated benchmarks. There is no evidence that the architectural speedup or quality trade-off persists for modern billion-parameter models, long contexts beyond 1024 tokens, instruction tuning, or realistic serving regimes.

Generated-text quality is assessed mainly through GPT-2-Large perplexity and unigram entropy. These proxies can miss coherence, diversity, memorization, and degeneration; no human evaluation or stronger distributional/text-quality metrics are provided, and decoding settings are insufficiently discussed.

Baseline coverage is narrow. The paper experimentally compares primarily against MDLM and GPT-2 Small, without evaluating relevant efficient alternatives such as block diffusion, any-subset autoregressive models, or optimized masked-model implementations.
Training-quality results come from single runs without uncertainty estimates. Several reported differences are small enough that seed variability could affect the conclusions.

The theoretical relationship to masked diffusion is intuitive but not formally established: the paper does not prove that the proposed objective and sampler preserve the intended diffusion distribution or characterize approximation error introduced by fixed-count uniform denoising.

Some reporting is inconsistent: latency columns labeled as milliseconds numerically correspond to seconds given the reported throughput, and the claimed GPT-2 comparison is not documented as completely as the MDLM comparison.

Distillation improves speed substantially, but MDLM+SDTT attains markedly better generative perplexity than PGM+SDTT while losing more entropy, making the claim of broadly superior distilled generation dependent on an incomplete quality trade-off.

strengths: The partition-based formulation and encoder–GroupSwap–decoder architecture are conceptually interesting and offer a clear way to avoid processing explicit MASK tokens.

The reported OpenWebText inference improvement over the reimplemented MDLM baseline is substantial—approximately 5–5.5× at matched sampling-step counts—and the paper measures both latency and throughput.
The paper includes useful architectural ablations, complementary-masking controls, downstream evaluations, training-cost measurements, sampling pseudocode, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is too narrow for the central efficiency claim. The main baseline is MDLM, with no convincing comparison against other recent efficient diffusion, any-order, blockwise, or parallel-generation approaches discussed in the related-work section.

Quality comparisons are substantially confounded by model capacity. On OpenWebText, a PGM with the baseline configuration underperforms MDLM, and the reported gains require more layers or a larger hidden dimension. Parameter counts, FLOPs, and carefully capacity- or training-compute-matched comparisons are not provided.

The evidence for generation quality is weak. Generative perplexity under GPT-2 Large plus unigram entropy cannot adequately detect copying, limited diversity, incoherence, or other degeneration. There is no human evaluation, MAUVE-style distributional evaluation, qualitative sampling analysis, or broader text-generation benchmark.

The paper reports only single training runs and no uncertainty for perplexity, generation quality, or downstream accuracy. This is especially problematic because architecture variants are selected after multiple experiments and several reported improvements are modest.

The claimed comparison with GPT-2 is inadequately documented: the manuscript emphasizes a 10.73× latency advantage with superior generative perplexity, but the appendix tables do not clearly provide the corresponding GPT-2 measurements, entropy, setup, or a comprehensive quality comparison.

There are multiple technical and reporting inconsistencies. The timing columns in Tables 3 and 5–8 are labeled milliseconds, but the reported throughput implies that the values are seconds. Some ImageNet latency/throughput entries also appear mutually inconsistent.

The formal presentation contains errors that impede reproducibility: the stated PGM cross-entropy weight inherits a negative alpha derivative despite being described as nonnegative, and Algorithm 1 appears off by one because it initializes a BOS token, has only L−1 remaining positions, but sets the per-step count to L/K.

The image experiments are explicitly preliminary and far from competitive quality, while the text experiments cover only relatively small models and two pretraining corpora. Consequently, the claimed generality across modalities and relevance to test-time scaling are speculative.

Training is slower and relies on dense attention masks; no efficient training implementation or scaling study is supplied. It remains unclear whether the inference advantage persists at modern model scales, different sequence lengths, or realistic deployment batch sizes.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically meaningful idea: replacing explicit mask-token processing with complementary token partitions and a specialized encoder–GroupSwap–decoder architecture.

The main efficiency evidence is compelling. On 1024-token OpenWebText generation, PGM provides roughly 5–5.5× lower latency and higher throughput than MDLM at matched sampling-step counts, while preserving or improving generative perplexity.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering LM1B, OpenWebText, downstream language tasks, distillation, and a preliminary ImageNet experiment. The complementary-masking and architecture ablations help identify where the gains arise.

The authors make a serious effort toward reproducibility by providing objectives, architectural details, sampling pseudocode, hyperparameters, compute costs, numerical-precision controls, and planned code/checkpoint release.

The paper is generally clear and appropriately acknowledges important limitations, including greater training cost, the need for a larger model on long-context OpenWebText, weaker benefits from SDTT, and preliminary image results.
weaknesses: The evidence for generation quality is not yet strong enough for a clear accept: text evaluation relies primarily on GPT-2-Large generative perplexity and unigram entropy, without stronger distributional metrics, human evaluation, or qualitative samples. These metrics may miss coherence, factuality, and diversity failures.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Comparisons center on MDLM and GPT-2 Small, while closely related any-order, any-subset, block-diffusion, and newer accelerated discrete-generation approaches are discussed but not evaluated. This makes the practical advantage over the broader design space unclear.

The strongest OpenWebText model increases hidden size to 1024 because the parameter-matched PGM does not consistently beat MDLM. Parameter counts and quality-versus-training/inference-FLOP comparisons are not reported clearly enough to fully characterize this tradeoff.

Most quality results appear to come from single training runs, with no uncertainty across seeds. Reported deviations cover timing measurements rather than the model-quality comparisons supporting the central claims.
The image experiment is explicitly preliminary and generally trails MDLM in FID at matched step counts; thus it offers limited support for the broader cross-modal framing.

Several reporting issues should be corrected: Table 5 labels latency as milliseconds although the throughput values imply seconds, the GPT-2 comparison underlying the claimed 10.73× speedup is not tabulated clearly, and Table 8 contains an apparently anomalous non-uniform throughput entry. These issues complicate verification of otherwise promising efficiency claims.

strengths: The central idea is novel and practically meaningful: replacing mask tokens with complementary partitions and a constrained encoder–GroupSwap–decoder architecture permits parallel, arbitrary-order generation while processing only already generated tokens at inference.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial and consistent across modalities: roughly 5–5.5× language-model throughput over MDLM and up to 7.5× image throughput over MaskGIT at matched sampling steps.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering LM1B, OpenWebText, ImageNet, likelihood-related metrics, sample-quality metrics, downstream language tasks, distillation, multiple sampling schedules, and training/inference costs.

Several comparisons are reasonably controlled: baselines are reproduced in the same setup, ImageNet models have closely matched parameter counts, and results are reported across sampling-step counts and guidance strengths.

The complementary-masking and architectural ablations provide useful evidence about where the improvements arise, while the successful application of SDTT demonstrates compatibility with existing acceleration methods.
weaknesses: The method is not specified with enough mathematical precision to verify the claimed absence of information leakage. The exact masks used by GroupSwap and decoder cross-attention are not formally defined, and the pseudocode treats the crucial prediction operation as an opaque `pgm_predict` call.

There appears to be an inconsistency in the training objective: a target in group 0 is predicted from group 1, whose expected size is p_t, yet Eq. (6) assigns it w(t) while claiming it has the same information as an MGM at time t, whose visible fraction is 1-p_t. The paper should derive the weighting carefully. The MDLM weight is also written as alpha'_t/(1-alpha_t), which is negative for the stated decreasing schedule, apparently missing a minus sign.

The strongest language-quality comparison is not capacity matched on OpenWebText: PGM needs 203M or 268M parameters to outperform the 170M MDLM. Although PGM remains faster, this weakens claims of an intrinsically better modeling objective and calls for parameter- and training-compute-matched scaling experiments.

Text generation quality is supported mainly by GPT-2-Large generative perplexity and unigram entropy. These metrics do not adequately capture coherence, diversity, memorization, or long-range quality; stronger distributional metrics, human evaluation, and representative samples are missing.

Efficiency reporting needs clarification. Several latency columns labeled milliseconds appear numerically to be seconds, and image throughput is measured at batch size 32 whereas latency is measured at batch size 1; the latter improves only modestly for PGM. Results across batch sizes, hardware, memory use, and optimized baselines would better establish practical speedups.

There are no repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates for perplexity, FID, or downstream accuracy. Code and checkpoints are only promised, and important implementation details remain underspecified, limiting current reproducibility.

strengths: The central idea—replacing masks with complementary token partitions and enforcing group-wise information isolation—is interesting and potentially useful. The encoder/GroupSwap/decoder architecture provides a concrete implementation that retains parallel, any-order decoding while reducing inference-time sequence lengths.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: roughly 5–5.5× over MDLM on OpenWebText and up to 7.5× over MaskGIT on ImageNet at comparable sampling quality. Evaluating both language and image generation strengthens the case that the idea is not modality-specific.

The paper includes useful architecture ablations, complementary-masking controls, training-cost measurements, downstream language tasks, multiple sampling schedules, and experiments combining PGM with distillation.
The manuscript is generally understandable and candidly acknowledges increased parameter counts, slower training, stability spikes, and the absence of experiments beyond context length 1024.
weaknesses: The strongest quality comparisons are not capacity-matched. On OpenWebText, the 12-layer, 768-dimensional PGM underperforms the 170M-parameter MDLM; improvements require 203M or 268M parameters. This weakens the claim that the modeling approach itself improves quality, and no compute- or parameter-matched scaling study is provided.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Language generation is assessed primarily using GPT-2-Large perplexity and unigram entropy on only 1,024 samples, without stronger distributional, semantic, human, or qualitative evaluations. The downstream models are also small and weak, so modest task-score differences are not compelling evidence of practical language-model quality.

Important recent or structurally relevant alternatives are discussed but not evaluated, including block diffusion, any-subset autoregressive models, and hybrid approaches such as Eso-LMs. Comparisons only against MDLM and MaskGIT do not establish the method's competitiveness with the broader efficient-generation literature.

There is a concerning inconsistency in the central formulation. The text defines group 0 as clean and group 1 as masked, so predictions at group-1 positions conditioned on group 0 appear to correspond to the MGM task at time t. Equation 6 instead assigns w(t) to group 0 and w(1-t) to group 1. The paper does not resolve this apparent reversal or state unambiguously what was implemented.

The claimed likelihood evaluation is under-specified. The number of Monte Carlo samples, estimator variance, and uncertainty are omitted, while differences as small as 0.09 perplexity are interpreted as improvements. No repeated training runs or confidence intervals are reported for perplexity, downstream accuracy, FID, or generative perplexity.

Several reporting errors undermine confidence in the empirical presentation. Tables 6 and 7 label multi-second sampling latencies as milliseconds; Table 7 contains an apparent copy error where a throughput value is placed in the latency column; and the text contains multiple typographical or notation errors. These issues make the headline efficiency numbers harder to audit.

The throughput results are tied to one A100 implementation and batch size, with no memory measurements, batch-size scaling, optimized baseline analysis, or end-to-end accounting beyond model sampling. The paper therefore demonstrates an implementation-specific speed advantage more clearly than a general systems advantage.

The proposed architecture makes training slower and relies on dense attention masks despite claiming exploitable sparsity. Code and models are only promised for future release, and important implementation details—particularly the exact objective and likelihood estimator—are insufficiently precise for confident reproduction.

The image study uses only one tokenizer, dataset, and baseline, and both models are trained for 500k steps rather than the referenced 2M-step recipe. The absence of learning curves, multiple seeds, and comparisons to stronger modern image generators limits conclusions about quality and convergence.

Overall, the work has a promising idea and notable preliminary results, but the formulation inconsistency, capacity-confounded comparisons, narrow quality evaluation, missing uncertainty, and insufficient baseline coverage leave the main claims less convincingly supported than expected for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The core idea is novel and practically important: replacing mask tokens with complementary partitions and enforcing information separation architecturally enables parallel, arbitrary-order generation while avoiding computation on unknown positions.

The efficiency gains are large and convincingly demonstrated across modalities: roughly 5–5.5× higher text throughput than MDLM and 7.5× higher ImageNet throughput than MaskGIT at comparable quality. Increasing PGM to 64 image-sampling steps yields better FID while retaining a 3.9× speedup.

The evaluation is broad and generally careful, covering LM1B, OpenWebText, ImageNet, validation likelihood bounds, sample quality, downstream tasks, distillation, latency, throughput, training cost, and longer-context inference.
The image comparison is especially persuasive because PGM and MaskGIT have closely matched parameter counts and are trained within the same codebase and setup.

Useful ablations examine encoder/decoder balance, query initialization, complementary masking, sampling schedules, numerical precision, and training stability. These help separate gains from denser supervision and gains from the proposed architecture.
The paper is clearly motivated and well organized, with an understandable architectural description, algorithms, extensive tables, and candid discussion of training overhead and scaling limitations.
Compatibility with existing masked-model samplers and SDTT distillation increases the likely usefulness and impact of the method.
weaknesses: The strongest OpenWebText quality result uses 268M parameters versus 170M for MDLM. Although PGM remains much faster, this prevents a clean capacity-matched conclusion about modeling quality; the equal-width 12-layer PGM underperforms MDLM at 200k steps, while the 16-layer model has more parameters.

The text-generation evidence relies heavily on GPT-2-Large generative perplexity and unigram entropy. These metrics do not adequately measure coherence, factuality, repetition beyond unigram statistics, or diversity; MAUVE-style metrics, human evaluation, and qualitative samples would strengthen the quality claim.

The empirical scale is modest for a language-modeling architecture paper: models are at most 268M parameters, trained only up to context length 1024. The 4096-token experiment measures inference throughput without training or quality evaluation, so behavior at modern model scales remains uncertain.

Comparisons focus mainly on MDLM and MaskGIT. Direct empirical comparisons with recent efficient or hybrid alternatives discussed in related work, such as block diffusion and any-subset or hybrid AR–MGM models, would better establish the method's position on the broader quality–latency frontier.

Reported results appear to come from single training runs, with no uncertainty over validation perplexity, downstream accuracy, FID, or generative perplexity. This makes small quality differences—such as ImageNet FID 5.54 versus 5.35—hard to interpret statistically.

The theoretical presentation is comparatively light: the paper motivates the complementary objective intuitively but does not formally characterize the distribution learned by PGM, prove consistency, or clearly derive the likelihood bound used for PGM evaluation.

Training is currently slower and requires specialized dense attention masks; the promised benefit from block-sparse kernels is plausible but not demonstrated. The method also shows training-loss spikes and different precision requirements, which may complicate scaling.

Reproducibility is good at the descriptive level, but code and checkpoints are only promised rather than provided, and there are minor reporting errors, including an apparent duplicated latency/throughput value in Table 7.
